tips.title: Choosing the Right Glue for Different Plastics
tips.text: For polystyrene, use Tamiya Extra Thin Cement (Item 87001) to melt the plastic together. For ABS parts, switch to Tamiya Cement (Item 87003) due to its ABS-compatible solvents. Super Glue works well for both but sets instantly, so use sparingly with precise application. For complex repairs, mix Super Glue with baking soda for a putty-like filler.

tips.title: Selecting the Correct Paint Type
tips.text: Acrylics like Vallejo Model Air and Model Color offer ease of use, quick drying, and wide color selection. Enamels like Tamiya Acrylic Paints provide excellent coverage and durability but take longer to dry. Lacquers like AMMO by Mig Jimenez offer a glossy finish but require a suitable thinner and careful application to prevent runs.

tips.title: Choosing the Right Sandpaper Grits
tips.text: Use 240-grit sandpaper for initial sanding of joints and filling. After filling with Tamiya Putty or Vallejo Plastic Putty, use 400-grit for smoothing. For fine sanding before painting, use 600-grit to avoid scratches. Always wet sand to avoid clogging and use a sanding block for even pressure.

tips.title: Filler for Gaps: Tamiya Putty vs Vallejo Plastic Putty
tips.text: Tamiya Putty (Item 87050) is easy to apply and sands smoothly, but it shrinks slightly on drying. Vallejo Plastic Putty (71.041) fills larger gaps without shrinking but can be harder to sand smooth. For best results, use Vallejo for deep gaps, let it dry, then fill smaller gaps with Tamiya Putty before sanding.

tips.title: Photo-Etch vs Resin Detail Parts
tips.text: Photo-etch (PE) from brands like Eduard offers intricate detail but requires careful handling and bending. Use a PE bending tool and tweezers for precise manipulation. Resin detail parts (e.g., from ICM) provide pre-shaped details but may require drilling for attachment. Choose PE for complex details like Cockpit Furniture, and resin for bulky items like Antennae or Access Handles.
